## Decision Summary

A scan engine must be designated for the Platform Gainwell Inbound File Scanning Service capability ([GUID-SEC-CLOUD-FILE-SCAN-2.6.11](../../strategy/guidance/security/Cloud-and-Infrastructure/GUID-SEC-CLOUD-FILE-SCAN-2.6.11.md)). Three options were evaluated: ClamAV on AWS Lambda (open-source), Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3, and a commercial AV SDK deployed on Lambda. This ADR documents the trade-offs and proposes a decision for Security Architecture review.

> **Note**: This ADR is **Proposed** pending Security Architecture and Security Domain EA Lead review. The outcome governs the Solution Building Block (SBB) authored in Phase E–F for realizing the file scanning ABB. The architectural pattern defined in [GUID-SEC-CLOUD-FILE-SCAN-2.6.11](../../strategy/guidance/security/Cloud-and-Infrastructure/GUID-SEC-CLOUD-FILE-SCAN-2.6.11.md) and [GUID-SEC-CLOUD-FILE-SCAN-RAD-3.6.04](../../strategy/guidance/security/Cloud-and-Infrastructure/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-CLOUD-FILE-SCAN-RAD-3.6.04.md) is engine-agnostic and applies regardless of this decision.

[decisions/security/ADR-SEC-003-FILE-SCAN-inbound-file-scanning-engine.md#business-context]

### Business Context

Platform Gainwell handles Protected Health Information (PHI) and Personally Identifiable Information (PII) for state Medicaid programs and healthcare operations. External partners, internal systems, and end-user applications submit files to Platform Gainwell storage volumes (S3 buckets, EFS, database systems) across multiple ingest channels.

Currently, no platform-wide control mandates malware or virus scanning of inbound file streams before they reach destination storage. This creates material risk of malicious content — trojans, ransomware, weaponized documents — entering Platform Gainwell data systems through the ingest boundary, potentially compromising PHI stores and downstream systems.

The Enterprise Architecture Practice has defined the Inbound File Scanning Service capability (AB#850549) and its governing ABB. This ADR governs the selection of the antivirus/malware scan engine to realize that capability.

[decisions/security/ADR-SEC-003-FILE-SCAN-inbound-file-scanning-engine.md#technical-context]

### Technical Context

- Platform Gainwell's primary cloud platform is Amazon Web Services (AWS)
- Ingest channels in v1 scope include: AWS Transfer Family (SFTP), S3 direct PUT, and API Gateway file uploads
- The AWS Solutions Library provides a validated reference implementation using AWS Transfer Family Managed Workflows with ClamAV on Lambda: [aws-solutions-library-samples/guidance-for-detecting-malware-threats-using-aws-transfer-family-managed-workflows-on-aws](https://github.com/aws-solutions-library-samples/guidance-for-detecting-malware-threats-using-aws-transfer-family-managed-workflows-on-aws)
- The governing ABB requires: fail-closed staging intercept, daily minimum definition refresh, immutable scan result tagging, quarantine store enforcement, and real-time SOC alerting
- The scan engine is deployed as a containerized AWS Lambda function (Docker image in ECR) or as an AWS-native managed service

[decisions/security/ADR-SEC-003-FILE-SCAN-inbound-file-scanning-engine.md#problem-statement]

### Problem Statement

The organization must select one scan engine approach to implement across all Platform Gainwell ingest channels. The selection must balance detection effectiveness, operational burden, cost, AWS integration depth, definition currency automation, and long-term supportability.
page_texts.9:
[decisions/security/ADR-SEC-003-FILE-SCAN-inbound-file-scanning-engine.md#decision-drivers]

### Decision Drivers

- 🔒 **HIPAA Compliance**: §164.308(a)(1) requires identification of threats to PHI, including malicious code delivered via file transfer
- 📋 **NIST 800-53 SI-3**: Malicious Code Protection — requires malicious code protection mechanisms at information system entry points with automatic updates
- 📋 **NIST 800-53 SI-3(2)**: Automatic Updates — definitions must refresh automatically
- ⚡ **AWS Integration Depth**: Solution must integrate natively with Transfer Family Managed Workflows, S3 event notifications, EventBridge, Lambda, and ECR without custom middleware
- 💰 **Cost at Scale**: Solution must remain cost-effective at Platform Gainwell's expected ingest volumes across all channels
- 🔄 **Definition Currency Automation**: Signature refresh must be fully automated with no manual operational steps
- 🧩 **Multi-Channel Coverage**: The same scan engine must be applicable uniformly across all three v1 ingest patterns (Transfer Family, S3 event, API Gateway)
- 🛠 **Operational Observability**: The scan execution path must emit structured logs compatible with the platform's CloudWatch and SIEM integration

[decisions/security/ADR-SEC-003-FILE-SCAN-inbound-file-scanning-engine.md#option-1-clamav-on-aws-lambda-containerized-open-source]

### Option 1: ClamAV on AWS Lambda (Containerized, Open-Source)

**Description**: Deploy ClamAV — the open-source antivirus engine maintained by Cisco Talos — as a containerized AWS Lambda function. The container image (including ClamAV binary and virus definitions) is stored in Amazon ECR. An EventBridge Scheduler rule triggers AWS CodeBuild on a daily minimum cadence to rebuild the container image with the latest ClamAV definitions and publish to ECR. The Lambda function is updated to reference the new image. This is the approach documented in the AWS Solutions Library reference implementation.

**Architecture fit**: This option directly realizes the definition currency pipeline pattern described in [GUID-SEC-CLOUD-FILE-SCAN-RAD-3.6.04](../../strategy/guidance/security/Cloud-and-Infrastructure/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-CLOUD-FILE-SCAN-RAD-3.6.04.md) using the EventBridge Scheduler → CodeBuild → ECR → Lambda update chain.

**Pros**:

- ✅ **Zero incremental licensing cost** — ClamAV is Apache 2.0 licensed; no per-scan or per-GB charges beyond Lambda, ECR, and CodeBuild
- ✅ **AWS Solutions Library validated** — AWS has published and maintains a deployable reference implementation; reduced implementation risk
- ✅ **Deep Transfer Family integration** — natively invoked within Transfer Family Managed Workflows as a custom processing step
- ✅ **Full control over scan logic** — container image customization allows tuning of archive recursion depth, file size limits, and scan timeout behavior
- ✅ **Fully automated definition update pipeline** — EventBridge → CodeBuild → ECR chain is well-understood and auditable
- ✅ **Works uniformly across all three v1 ingest patterns** — Lambda can be invoked by Managed Workflows, S3 Event Notifications, and API Gateway triggers
- ✅ **Structured scan output** — Lambda returns structured JSON result; CloudWatch log integration is native

**Cons**:

- ❌ **Definition currency is community-maintained** — ClamAV definitions are updated by Cisco Talos; detection rate for emerging threats may lag commercial engines, particularly for zero-day malware
- ❌ **Operational ownership of update pipeline** — Platform Engineering owns the CodeBuild/ECR refresh pipeline; pipeline failures require operational response
- ❌ **Container image size** — ClamAV with full definitions produces large container images (~500MB+), which increases Lambda cold start time and ECR storage cost
- ❌ **False negative risk on targeted threats** — ClamAV is a signature-based engine; heuristic and behavioral detection capabilities are limited compared to commercial alternatives

---
page_texts.12:
[decisions/security/ADR-SEC-003-FILE-SCAN-inbound-file-scanning-engine.md#option-2-amazon-guardduty-malware-protection-for-s3]

### Option 2: Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3

**Description**: Enable Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 — an AWS-native managed service that scans S3 objects for malware when they are uploaded, without requiring custom Lambda functions or definition management. GuardDuty uses AWS threat intelligence and malware scanning infrastructure. Scan results are published as GuardDuty findings and as S3 object tags.

**Architecture fit**: This option eliminates the Lambda scan execution and definition pipeline components. The staging bucket triggers native GuardDuty scanning on object PUT. GuardDuty tags the object with scan result; a promotion gate checks the tag before allowing downstream access. EventBridge rules on GuardDuty findings route `INFECTED` alerts to the SOC.

**Pros**:

- ✅ **Zero operational definition management** — AWS manages definition updates entirely; no CodeBuild pipeline, no ECR image rebuilds
- ✅ **AWS-native integration** — direct S3 bucket association; no Lambda function required for the scan step
- ✅ **AWS threat intelligence** — backed by AWS's global threat intelligence, not limited to community signatures
- ✅ **Automatic scan result tagging** — GuardDuty natively tags scanned S3 objects with `GuardDutyMalwareScanStatus: NO_THREATS_FOUND` or `THREATS_FOUND`
- ✅ **Reduced operational surface** — no container image lifecycle, no ECR registry management, no update pipeline maintenance
- ✅ **Per-GB pricing model** — cost scales directly with actual ingest volume, no fixed Lambda concurrency reservation required

**Cons**:

- ❌ **S3-only — does not cover Transfer Family directly** — GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 is triggered on S3 object PUTs; Transfer Family Managed Workflow integration would require a hybrid approach (GuardDuty scans staging bucket; workflow checks tag result)
- ❌ **No synchronous scan result in workflow context** — GuardDuty scan is asynchronous; Managed Workflows cannot block file promotion waiting for a GuardDuty result; a polling or event-driven gate is required, adding latency and complexity
- ❌ **Limited scan customization** — archive recursion depth, size thresholds, and scan timeout behavior are not configurable by the customer
- ❌ **Tag schema differs from enterprise standard** — GuardDuty uses its own tag keys; the enterprise scan result tag schema defined in the ABB (`scan-status`, `scan-engine-version`, etc.) would require a translation layer
- ❌ **Per-object pricing at scale** — at high ingest volumes, per-GB pricing may exceed ClamAV Lambda cost
- ❌ **Not applicable to API Gateway ingest pattern** — API Gateway uploads that bypass S3 direct PUT require an additional S3 write step before GuardDuty can trigger

---
page_texts.13:
[decisions/security/ADR-SEC-003-FILE-SCAN-inbound-file-scanning-engine.md#option-3-commercial-av-sdk-on-lambda-eg-trend-micro-file-security-sophos-intelix]

### Option 3: Commercial AV SDK on Lambda (e.g., Trend Micro File Security, Sophos Intelix)

**Description**: Deploy a commercial antivirus SDK (such as Trend Micro File Security for Lambda or Sophos Intelix) as a containerized Lambda function. Commercial SDKs provide higher detection rates, behavioral analysis, and SLA-backed definition updates compared to ClamAV.

**Architecture fit**: Same Lambda-based execution model as Option 1; the scan engine binary is replaced with the commercial SDK. Definition updates are delivered via the vendor's update mechanism (often a cloud API call rather than a full image rebuild).

**Pros**:

- ✅ **Higher detection rates** — commercial engines include behavioral, heuristic, and machine-learning detection layers beyond signature matching
- ✅ **SLA-backed definition currency** — vendors provide contractual update frequency and response time for new threats
- ✅ **Vendor support** — commercial support contract provides incident escalation path if a threat signature is missed
- ✅ **Same integration model as Option 1** — Lambda-based invocation works uniformly across all three v1 ingest patterns

**Cons**:

- ❌ **Per-scan or per-GB licensing cost** — commercial SDKs carry recurring licensing fees that scale with ingest volume; cost modeling required before commitment
- ❌ **Procurement cycle required** — no current enterprise license exists for a Lambda-deployable commercial AV SDK; procurement, legal review, and security approval are required
- ❌ **Vendor lock-in** — switching engines later requires re-implementation of the scan function and definition update pipeline
- ❌ **SDK integration complexity** — commercial SDKs require vendor-specific API integration; behavior on edge cases (zip bombs, polyglot files) must be validated
- ❌ **Longer time-to-implement** — procurement cycle adds timeline risk compared to open-source or AWS-native options

[decisions/security/ADR-SEC-003-FILE-SCAN-inbound-file-scanning-engine.md#decision-outcome]

## Decision Outcome

**Proposed Chosen Option**: **Option 1 — ClamAV on AWS Lambda (Containerized, Open-Source)**

**Rationale**: ClamAV on Lambda is the recommended starting point for the following reasons:

1. **AWS Solutions Library validation** substantially reduces implementation risk. The reference implementation is deployable, documented, and maintained.
2. **Zero incremental licensing cost** is appropriate for the v1 capability rollout; cost remains predictable as ingest volumes scale.
3. **Uniform multi-channel coverage** — ClamAV Lambda can be invoked synchronously within Transfer Family Managed Workflows, by S3 event notifications, and by API Gateway triggers using the same container image, satisfying the uniform coverage requirement of the governing ABB.
4. **Full definition currency automation** via the EventBridge Scheduler → CodeBuild → ECR chain satisfies NIST 800-53 SI-3(2) without manual operational steps.
5. **Detection gap is accepted and bounded for v1** — ClamAV provides signature-based detection of known malware, trojans, and virus families via Cisco Talos intelligence. Independent analyses (VirusTotal telemetry studies; academic comparisons such as Botacin et al.) consistently place ClamAV's detection rate for novel/emerging samples at approximately **65–75% of what commercial engines detect**, representing a 20–30 percentage point gap for threats not yet catalogued in the Talos signature database. The primary threat scenario for Platform Gainwell ingest channels is **commodity malware and weaponized documents from external partners** — threat families for which Talos maintains current signatures — not targeted zero-day attacks. The residual false-negative risk is therefore accepted for known-threat-profile ingest traffic, supplemented by GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 as a secondary async scan layer on the staging bucket (see Mitigations). This accepted risk is explicitly bounded to v1; it does not apply if the threat profile classification changes.

  > **Note on endpoint protection comparisons:** Enterprise EDR/XDR platforms (e.g., CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender, Elastic Security) achieve 99.3–100% protection in AV-Comparatives Business Security Test March–April 2026. These figures are not directly comparable to ClamAV's file-scan context — they represent endpoint agents with behavioral detection, ML classification, and cloud sandboxing running on managed hosts. They are not deployable as Lambda-based file scanning functions and are therefore not applicable alternatives for this ingest-boundary architecture.

**Migration path**: The Lambda function container image can be replaced with Option 3 (commercial SDK, e.g., Trend Micro Vision One File Security or Sophos Intelix) without architectural changes to the staging/landing zone pattern, promotion gate, quarantine store, or SOC alerting chain. **This migration SHALL be initiated if any of the following trigger criteria are met:**

- SOC confirms **two or more false-negative events** (malware that passed ClamAV scan and reached destination storage) within any 90-day rolling window
- A HIPAA Security Risk Assessment identifies malware ingestion at the file ingest boundary as a contributing factor to a security incident
- A Cisco Talos Kantara certification lapse or Talos threat intelligence SLA is downgraded, reducing definition currency below the ABB's daily minimum requirement
- Platform Gainwell's threat profile classification is elevated to include targeted attacks or advanced persistent threats (APTs) against the ingest boundary
- A regulatory body (CMS, state Medicaid authority) explicitly requires a commercial AV engine or specific detection-rate threshold for HIPAA safeguard compliance
page_texts.15:
[decisions/security/ADR-SEC-003-FILE-SCAN-inbound-file-scanning-engine.md#implementation]

### Implementation

- 🎯 **Key Steps**:
  1. Create feature branch and IaC formation in `iac/terraform/formations/aws/` for the file scan stack
  2. Build ClamAV container image with definitions and publish to ECR (`clamav-scanner` repository)
  3. Deploy Lambda function from ECR image with reserved concurrency and VPC configuration
  4. Configure Transfer Family Managed Workflow to invoke ClamAV Lambda as a custom step
  5. Configure S3 event notification trigger for direct-PUT ingest channels
  6. Implement EventBridge Scheduler → CodeBuild definition refresh pipeline (daily cadence minimum)
  7. Configure EventBridge rule on `scan-status: INFECTED` tag + SNS topic for SOC alerting
  8. Enable CloudWatch log group with immutable retention policy for scan audit trail
  9. Apply bucket policies: deny promotion from staging without `scan-status: CLEAN` tag; deny all access to quarantine store except SOC role

- 📊 **Success Criteria**:
  - 100% of files on in-scope ingest channels receive a scan result before promotion
  - `INFECTED` detection triggers SOC alert within 5-minute SLO
  - Definition currency pipeline executes successfully on daily schedule with zero manual intervention
  - Fail-closed behavior confirmed: scan engine unavailability prevents file promotion

page_texts.17:
[decisions/security/ADR-SEC-003-FILE-SCAN-inbound-file-scanning-engine.md#-positive]

### ✅ Positive

- Platform Gainwell achieves ingest-boundary malware scanning coverage across all v1 ingest channels
- NIST 800-53 SI-3 and SI-3(2) architectural intent is satisfied for inbound file handling
- HIPAA risk for malicious content delivered via file transfer is materially reduced
- SOC gains real-time visibility into `INFECTED` ingest events with structured alert data
- ClamAV architecture established in v1 is replaceable with a commercial engine without re-architecting the surrounding platform pattern
page_texts.18:
[decisions/security/ADR-SEC-003-FILE-SCAN-inbound-file-scanning-engine.md#-negative]

### ❌ Negative

- Platform Engineering owns ongoing operational responsibility for the CodeBuild/ECR definition refresh pipeline; pipeline failures require active monitoring and response
- ClamAV signature-based detection will not catch novel, targeted malware that has not yet been catalogued in the community definition database
- ClamAV container images are large; Lambda cold starts will be longer than for lightweight functions; concurrency pre-warming may be required for latency-sensitive ingest channels
page_texts.19:
[decisions/security/ADR-SEC-003-FILE-SCAN-inbound-file-scanning-engine.md#-neutral]

### ⚪ Neutral

- The scan engine decision does not affect the staging/landing zone architecture, quarantine store design, SOC alert routing, or audit logging patterns — those are defined by the ABB and apply regardless of engine choice
- Future expansion to Kafka binary payload and database LOB scanning (deferred from v1) will require a separate ADR addendum addressing engine applicability to non-S3 data streams

[decisions/security/ADR-SEC-003-FILE-SCAN-inbound-file-scanning-engine.md#-risks]

### ⚠️ Risks

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Severity |
|---|---|---|---|
| ClamAV fails to detect novel/emerging malware (est. 20–30% detection gap vs. commercial engines for unknown samples) | Low | High | Medium |
| GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 not enabled on staging bucket — no secondary scan layer | Low | High | Medium |
| Definition refresh pipeline failure causes definition staleness | Medium | High | Medium |
| Lambda cold start latency degrades Transfer Family throughput SLA | Low | Medium | Low |
| Zip bomb / deeply nested archive causes Lambda timeout | Low | Medium | Low |
| Quarantine store access policy misconfiguration allows unauthorized access to infected PHI | Low | Critical | High |
page_texts.22:
[decisions/security/ADR-SEC-003-FILE-SCAN-inbound-file-scanning-engine.md#-mitigations]

### 🛡️ Mitigations

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| ClamAV detection gap (novel/emerging malware) | (1) Enable **Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3** on the staging bucket as a secondary async scan layer — GuardDuty uses AWS threat intelligence independent of Talos signatures, providing complementary coverage at no Lambda-side cost. For **S3 event-driven ingest patterns** (Patterns 2 and 3 in GUID-SEC-CLOUD-FILE-SCAN-RAD-3.6.04), a two-phase staging hold gate (delay promotion until both ClamAV and GuardDuty scans have returned results) MAY be implemented at the SBB level where ingest latency tolerance permits. For **Transfer Family Managed Workflow ingest** (Pattern 1), GuardDuty Malware Protection operates as a post-promotion async re-quarantine trigger only — Managed Workflow steps require a synchronous scan result and cannot block on an async GuardDuty response (see Option 2 CON in this ADR). In both cases, `GuardDuty:Malware:S3ObjectThreat` findings are routed to the SOC SNS topic alongside ClamAV `INFECTED` alerts. (2) Review ClamAV false-negative events in SOC detection telemetry quarterly. (3) Initiate Option 3 commercial SDK evaluation if any migration trigger criteria (defined above) are met. |
| No secondary scan layer on staging bucket | Enable GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 on the staging/landing bucket as described above; validate EventBridge routing of `GuardDuty:Malware:S3ObjectThreat` findings to SOC SNS topic |
| Definition staleness | CloudWatch alarm on definition timestamp delta > 24 hours; 48-hour escalation to SOC; CodeBuild pipeline failures trigger PagerDuty/SNS alert to Platform Engineering on-call |
| Lambda cold start latency | Configure Lambda provisioned concurrency for high-throughput ingest channels; benchmark at expected peak volume before production deployment |
| Zip bomb / archive depth | Configure ClamAV `MaxRecursion`, `MaxFiles`, `MaxFileSize` limits in clamd.conf; test with EICAR archive test vectors including nested archives |
| Quarantine store access | IaC policy test coverage for quarantine bucket deny-all-except-SOC; automated policy drift detection via AWS Config rule |

## Compliance Notes

| Framework | Requirement | How This Decision Addresses It |
|---|---|---|
| NIST 800-53 SI-3 | Malicious Code Protection — deploy malicious code protection at information system entry/exit points | ClamAV Lambda deployed at every ingest boundary before destination store access |
| NIST 800-53 SI-3(2) | Automatic Updates — update malicious code protection mechanisms automatically | EventBridge Scheduler → CodeBuild → ECR pipeline satisfies automatic daily update requirement |
| NIST 800-53 IR-6 | Incident Reporting — report incidents to appropriate organizational entities | `INFECTED` EventBridge events → SNS → SOC alert routing satisfies architectural incident reporting intent |
| NIST 800-53 AU-9 | Protection of Audit Information — protect audit records from unauthorized modification | Immutable CloudWatch log group + S3 Object Lock on audit trail satisfies this intent |
| HIPAA §164.308(a)(1) | Security Management Process — identify and protect against reasonably anticipated threats to PHI | Ingest-boundary malware scanning directly addresses this safeguard requirement |
